# WAF, Shield, Firewall Manager and Network Firewall: say it

<!-- speak:start id=edge-protection-s02 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** Do I need Shield Advanced, or are AWS WAF and Shield Standard enough?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** For many startups, Shield Standard plus AWS WAF is enough. Buy Shield Advanced when an attack's downtime or bill would cost more than the fee.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both Shield tiers protect you against DDoS attacks.

The difference is the help and the cost protection you get during a big attack.

It works like this. Shield Standard is on for every AWS customer, at no extra charge.

It handles the common network floods, like SYN floods.

Shield doesn't read the contents of web requests.

So against floods of web requests, you add AWS WAF rules.

Shield Advanced adds a response team at any hour, with Business or Enterprise Support.

You can request service credits when an attack makes your protected resources scale out.

The thing to watch is the price: three thousand dollars per month.

And it comes with a one-year subscription commitment.

In your case, I'd start with Shield Standard and AWS WAF on your public endpoints.

What would one hour of downtime cost you?

**Skeleton.** Standard on, free / web floods need AWS WAF / Advanced adds team and credits / monthly fee, one-year commitment

**Must say.**

- All AWS customers get the automatic protection of Shield Standard at no additional charge.
- Shield does not inspect the contents of web requests, so you use AWS WAF against HTTP GET or POST floods.
- Shield Advanced adds 24/7 support from the Shield Response Team, with a Business or Enterprise Support plan, and service credits that you request for attack charges.
- Shield Advanced costs $3,000 per month and has a 1-year subscription commitment.

**Do not say.**

- "Shield Standard works only after you turn it on". Say: All AWS customers get the automatic protection of Shield Standard, at no additional charge.
- "Shield Advanced protects all your resources automatically". Say: Shield Advanced protects only the resources you specify, in Shield Advanced or through a Firewall Manager policy.
- "Shield Standard stops HTTP floods on its own". Say: Shield does not inspect the contents of HTTP traffic. Use AWS WAF against HTTP GET or POST floods.

**Follow-up questions.**

- If an attack makes our servers scale out, who pays? With Shield Standard, you pay. With Shield Advanced, you can request a service credit for those charges. The resource must be protected before the attack: resources added during an attack are not eligible.
- Can we turn on Shield Advanced for one month around a launch? No. Shield Advanced has a 1-year subscription commitment, and subscriptions auto-renew annually.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=edge-protection-s01 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** The attack came from 1,400 addresses. Why can't we block those addresses?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** We can, but attackers change addresses. So we limit how fast each address signs in, and check sign-ins against stolen passwords.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: we can, but the attacker then uses new addresses.

So we block the behavior, not the list.

It works like this. AWS WAF is a set of rules at our front end that reads every request.

One rule counts the sign-in requests from each address.

An address over the limit is blocked until it slows down.

A second rule checks each sign-in against a database of stolen passwords.

It works even when each address sends only a few tries.

The thing to watch is real users who share one address.

An office behind one address counts as one sender, so we tune the limit.

We test in count mode first, then switch to block.

In your case, Ostell Bank's supervisors probably sign in from one office.

How many of them sign in from the same office address?

**Skeleton.** block behavior, not a list / count each address, block fast ones / check stolen passwords / shared office address, tune limit

**Must say.**

- A rate-based rule counts the requests of each address and rate limits the ones that come too fast.
- An address over the limit is blocked until its request rate falls below the threshold.
- The account takeover prevention managed rule group inspects login attempts and checks them against a stolen credential database.
- By default the rule counts by request IP address, so users behind one shared address share one count.

**Do not say.**

- "a network ACL can hold all of those addresses". Say: A network ACL has 20 rules per network ACL by default, so it can't hold a long list of addresses.
- "the rate rule stops every attacker". Say: The rule counts each address on its own. Many addresses that each stay under the limit are not blocked.
- "the rule blocks at exactly the limit". Say: AWS WAF rate limiting does not guarantee an exact limit match. It is meant to control high request rates.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can we put the addresses in a block list anyway? Yes, for addresses you know are bad. An AWS WAF IP set holds up to 10,000 entries, each an address or a range. A network ACL is the wrong place: it has 20 rules per network ACL by default. A list stops nothing when the attacker changes addresses.
- Do we have to add these rules again in every new account? No. With a Firewall Manager policy, when a new account joins the organization, Firewall Manager automatically applies the policy to the resources in its scope.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
